title: Streaming space for additive \(L_\infty\) estimation
formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the optimal worst-case bit space for a one-pass randomized streaming algorithm that returns only an estimate \(z\) of \(\|f\|_\infty\), with \[\Pr\!\left[|z-\|f\|_\infty|\le\frac{\|f\|_p}{k}\right]\ge\frac23.\] The bound must describe its dependence on domain size \(n\ge2\), update budget \(M\ge2\), accuracy parameter \(k\ge4\), norm flag \(p\in\{1,2\}\), and update mode \(b\in\{\mathrm{insert},\mathrm{difference}\}\), in the model below.
why: Separate the memory needed for one largest-magnitude estimate from the information needed to identify heavy coordinates, while accounting for error scale, domain size and cancellation.
status_note: Partially resolved historical source direction. The PODS 2016 paper explicitly reports an answer for insertion-only L1-relative maximum-frequency estimation, so that endpoint is not advertised here as a fresh open problem. The present full space characterization retains both source norms and update modes with explicit editorial conventions. Its complete current status was not established by the bounded 14 September 2026 search; source proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Cormode asks for reduced bit space for scalar \(L_\infty\) estimates under \(L_1\)- or \(L_2\)-scaled additive error, discussing insertions and differences of streams.

Bhattacharyya–Dey–Woodruff report improved maximum-frequency space and a resolution of the insertion-only \(L_1\) variant in their formulation. This is a partial resolution of the broader source direction.

sentences: The output is a single estimate of the largest absolute coordinate of a streamed frequency vector.
The allowed additive error is one over k times the final L1 or L2 norm.
Insertion-only streams and signed differences of two streams are distinct modes of the same resource question.
The target is a tight bit-space characterization in the domain size, update budget and accuracy.
A 2016 paper reports resolving the insertion-only L1 part, while this review does not certify a complete characterization of all cases.

definitions: Parameters \(n,M,k\) are integers supplied in binary before the stream, together with the two flags. The frequency vector starts at \(f=0\in\mathbb Z^n\). There are at most \(M\) updates \((i,\Delta)\), where \(1\le i\le n\). In insert mode every \(\Delta=1\); in difference mode \(\Delta\in\{-1,1\}\), and update \((i,\Delta)\) replaces \(f_i\) by \(f_i+\Delta\). Negative intermediate and final frequencies are allowed in difference mode. Equivalently, positively and negatively tagged insertions describe the difference of two streams, with their combined length bounded by \(M\). Only this bound, not the actual stream length, is known in advance. Set \(\|f\|_1=\sum_i|f_i|\), \(\|f\|_2=(\sum_i f_i^2)^{1/2}\), and \(\|f\|_\infty=\max_i|f_i|\). The additive tolerance is scaled by the final vector, not by the total number of updates; cancellation therefore matters. At the end, output one rational number \(z\) as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator. No coordinate identity or list of heavy items is requested. On \(f=0\), the success event requires exactly \(z=0\). The fixed stream is chosen independently of the algorithm’s private independent fair random bits. There is one terminal query, with success at least \(2/3\) separately on every valid stream; there is no requirement of simultaneous success at all prefixes. Use a uniform randomized multitape streaming machine with one fixed finite program for all parameters, no advice, no public random table and no oracle. The parameter header is read-only. An update is available in a read-only buffer until the machine advances to the next update, after which earlier updates cannot be revisited. Every work-tape bit, stored random bit or seed, counter, index, table and input-dependent retained state counts toward space, including all scratch space used during processing and final decoding. Input and write-only output cells do not count; copies do. Address and head-position information accessible to the algorithm that can carry input-dependent state is charged. The unreadable physical position of the one-way stream is not work memory; the number of updates already consumed is not supplied as a free clock. Random bits cannot be reread unless retained. The machine must halt on every valid finite stream and every random tape; computation time is unrestricted. Space is the maximum number of charged bits over all such streams and random tapes for the given parameters, not its expectation. Bounds may be piecewise over parameter regimes and must use ordinary asymptotic notation with all logarithmic factors exposed. The reciprocal-integer accuracy convention \(\epsilon=1/k\), finite update budget, private randomness and bit accounting make the source’s qualitative space question precise.
answer_criterion: Supply a tight asymptotic space characterization across the complete parameter domain and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean. It must include uniform algorithms attaining the stated upper bounds, their terminal-error and worst-case-space guarantees, and matching lower bounds for every algorithm in the same model, up to constants independent of all parameters and flags. A one-sided bound, a bound only for identifying heavy items, a word count hiding bit costs, or a result for only one norm or update mode does not determine the whole characterization. This is an asymptotic resource target: the benchmark does not apply an additive 1/100 tolerance to big-O or big-Theta bounds.

context_blocks.text: The largest absolute frequency is a scalar statistic. Identifying which item attains it can require additional information about a large item domain. The source asks whether that distinction can reduce memory when an additive error measured against the full frequency vector is allowed.

The two norms specify different accuracy requirements. For \(f=(3,-2,0)\), the target value is three, while the error scale is either \(5/k\) or \(\sqrt{13}/k\). For a difference stream, many updates can cancel, so an error proportional to the number of processed updates can be much larger than the permitted error.

This card retains both error scales and both update settings from the source as flags in one space-complexity characterization. It asks for their full dependence on the domain, stream budget and accuracy, rather than for a new yes/no claim that every historical bound remains unimproved. The exact finite-input and randomness conventions are editorial specifications.

Bhattacharyya, Dey and Woodruff explicitly report answering the insertion-only \(L_1\)-error part of the 2006 question. For maximum-frequency estimation they report \(O(\epsilon^{-1}\log\epsilon^{-1}+\log n+\log\log t)\) bits, where \(t\) is the stream length, and describe optimality in their stated regimes. Their result is recorded as existing progress, not as an unsolved insertion-only endpoint.

That result does not by itself supply the \(L_2\)-relative or signed-difference cases. In particular, insertion-only \(\|f\|_1\) equals the number of updates, whereas cancellation destroys that equality in a difference stream. A theorem’s norm, update promise, scalar versus item output, and parameter restrictions must all match before it can be counted toward the full target.

The original page explicitly distinguishes bit space from a count of machine words: random-function descriptions and counters also consume memory. The reviewed card preserves that distinction. The requested comparison is therefore about complete memory usage, not only the number of stored counters.

A full characterization would identify which memory costs arise from maintaining frequency magnitudes and which arise from recovering item names. It would clarify the value of scalar summaries for comparing streams over large domains and the cost of allowing deletions or cancellation.
